definitions.meaning: to obscure something is to hide it from view
to travel a distance, as in getting over so many miles of ground
a journalist reports on an event, as in giving news of a story

explanation.definitionFit: Three senses of one word: to hide, to traverse a distance, and to report on news as a journalist does.

parts.note: not a seamstress but the Egyptian queen whose name is on the London obelisk called her Needle, and who died from a self-inflicted snake bite

explanation.surface: A seamstress who accidentally stabbed herself to death with her needle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Needlewoman' looks like a sewer; it is the queen behind the obelisk on London's Thames Embankment, and the puncture is the asp's bite.
explanation.definitionFit: The Egyptian queen is named on the London obelisk and killed herself with an asp's bite.

clue.text: Traitor is a person of consequence — execute her

parts.note: a VIP is a very important person

indicators.note: to execute is to behead, so the word her loses its head letter

explanation.surface: An order to put to death a woman judged a traitor and a notable figure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'execute' means cut off the head: HER loses its first letter to leave ER.
explanation.definitionFit: A treacherous person is called a snake, and this venomous snake is the usual figure for that betrayal.

clue.text: One supposes it may be ready

definitions.meaning: someone who reckons, that is supposes or calculates
a ready ... is a book of pre-calculated tables

explanation.definitionFit: Someone who reckons supposes or calculates, and a book of tables for quick sums is a ready one.

clue.text: Cavalryman must be a good swimmer

definitions.meaning: a trooper in the ..., a British household cavalry regiment
the person watching bathers at a pool or beach

explanation.definitionFit: A trooper of the Life Guards cavalry regiment, and also the beach attendant who rescues swimmers.

definitions.meaning: to idle or loiter
British slang 'use your ...' means use your head, from rhyming slang ... of bread = head

explanation.definitionFit: To loiter idly, and British slang for the head or good sense (rhyming slang: loaf of bread = head).

parts.note: time is often called the enemy, and here it appears personified as the old man with a scythe and hourglass

explanation.surface: A foe turning up in the flesh.
explanation.walkthrough: The saying 'time is the enemy' gives the enemy; 'in person' asks for its personification.
explanation.definitionFit: The traditional personification of time is an old bearded figure carrying a scythe and hourglass.

clue.text: Foreign coppers — find one a nuisance to pick up

indicators.note: in a down clue, picking up lifts the words a nuisance so they read from the bottom upwards

parts.note: a drag is a tedious nuisance
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: Police abroad treat you as an irritation to be collected.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to pick up' turns A DRAG upwards into GARDA; I follows. The Garda is the police force of Ireland.
explanation.definitionFit: Plural of the Irish word for a police officer, so they are police of another country.

indicators.note: pronounced signals that the word seller is to be heard as its sound-twin

parts.note: a seller spoken sounds like a cellar, and a cellar is an underground room

explanation.surface: A salesman speaks in a grovelling manner.
explanation.walkthrough: Two steps: 'pronounced' makes 'seller' sound like 'cellar', and a cellar is a BASEMENT. Ko-towing (kowtowing) is bowing deeply in submission.
explanation.definitionFit: Kowtowing is grovelling submission, a humbling or lowering of oneself.

parts.note: demi- is a prefix meaning half

indicators.note: the beginning of the word term is its first letter

explanation.surface: Quitting a job once the second half of the school term starts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'half-term' reads as a school holiday; split it into 'half' and 'term's beginning'.
explanation.definitionFit: To demit is an old or formal word for laying down an office, that is quitting it.

indicators.note: the men walk out of the cough-mixture, so their letters are removed

parts.note: an expectorant is medicine that loosens phlegm
OR, other ranks, is military shorthand for soldiers who are not officers

explanation.surface: Men abandon the cough syrup and look after a child instead.
explanation.walkthrough: 'leave' takes OR (other ranks) out of EXPECTORANT. 'with child' is an old phrase for pregnant.
explanation.definitionFit: Being pregnant means awaiting a baby, so an expectant mother is one carrying a child.

clue.text: True mathematician's starting to create a sphere

parts.note: real means genuine or true

indicators.note: the starting letter of the word mathematician is taken

explanation.surface: A genuine mathematician begins to build a globe.
explanation.definitionFit: A domain or field of activity is a sphere, as in one's sphere of influence.

definitions.meaning: Americans call the full stop punctuation mark by this name
a recurring stretch of time, such as a menstrual cycle

explanation.definitionFit: US English for a full stop, and also a recurring span of time such as a monthly cycle.

clue.text: State of alarm — danger signal later changed

parts.note: a red light or flag warns of danger

indicators.note: the letters of the word later are changed into a new order

explanation.surface: A warning light gets altered to come on afterwards.
explanation.definitionFit: The highest level of readiness for an emergency, a condition of full alarm.

definitions.meaning: Professor ... is the explorer-scientist in Conan Doyle's The Lost World
a contender who aims to take the title

explanation.definitionFit: Conan Doyle's fictional professor in The Lost World, and the contender who aims to take a title.

indicators.note: to cook is to doctor or rework, so the following words are rearranged

explanation.surface: A chef whips up the traditional bill of fare.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cook' looks like the chef; it is the anagram signal working on BEAT THE OLD.
explanation.definitionFit: A fixed-price set meal with limited choice, so a kind of restaurant bill of fare.

clue.text: Downhill racer's weight said to cause death

definitions.note: the 's stands for is, linking the definition to the wordplay

parts.note: a bob is the weight on a plumb line or pendulum

indicators.note: said signals that the word for killing is heard, not spelt

parts.note: to slay is to kill

explanation.surface: A downhill competitor's bulk is blamed for a fatality.
explanation.definitionFit: A steerable sled raced down an ice track, a vehicle that hurtles downhill.

indicators.note: almost means the last letter is lost

parts.note: 29 across is a father; the biblical King David's father was Jesse

explanation.surface: A father whose restraint is nearly on show.
explanation.walkthrough: 29 across is DADDY: David's daddy is Jesse, and 'almost' drops the final E. In falconry a jess is a strap on a hawk's leg.
explanation.definitionFit: In falconry, a short strap fastened round a hawk's leg to hold the bird.

clue.text: Nervous about games in the garden

definitions.note: a feature found in a garden, defined by where it is

indicators.note: about means the timid word goes around the word for games

parts.note: shy means timid or nervous
a rubber is a set of games in bridge or whist

explanation.surface: Feeling anxious about playing sport outdoors among the plants.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' signals the container. A rubber is a set of games in bridge or whist, a sense many solvers miss.
explanation.definitionFit: A planting of bushes is a common feature found in a garden.

definitions.meaning: a bottle with its stopper pulled out
corked wine is tainted, so wine that is not corked is unspoiled

explanation.definitionFit: A bottle with its stopper drawn, and, read as un-corked, wine free of cork taint.

clue.text: Starts to attack massed bumf on desk

indicators.note: the starts of the following words are taken, one letter from each

explanation.surface: Beginning an assault on a heap of paperwork on the desk.
explanation.walkthrough: Bumf is British slang for tedious paperwork.
explanation.definitionFit: A raised stand or reading desk in early churches from which scripture was read.

clue.text: Heat presents our most difficult puzzle

definitions.meaning: a qualifying round in a competition
the newspaper's qualifying puzzle for its crossword championship, so its hardest

explanation.definitionFit: A qualifying heat knocks out contestants, and the paper's championship qualifier was its toughest puzzle.

clue.text: Christmas present: a length of cloth

parts.note: now means at present
an ell is an old unit of length for cloth

explanation.surface: A Christmas gift of a piece of fabric.
explanation.walkthrough: 'present' is not a gift but the time now.
explanation.definitionFit: A word shouted in carols celebrating the season of Christ's birth.

definitions.meaning: to draw a vehicle in to the roadside
a knitted jumper

explanation.definitionFit: To pull a car in to the side, and a knitted jumper put on over the head.

definitions.meaning: ... are bets
the punt was the currency of Ireland before the euro

explanation.definitionFit: Bets placed, and the old Irish currency, which is foreign money to a British solver.

definitions.meaning: a spider's net for catching flies
one of Titania's fairies in Shakespeare's A Midsummer Night's Dream

explanation.definitionFit: A spider's net that snares insects, and a fairy attendant in A Midsummer Night's Dream.

clue.text: Pressed one's suit and married without love twice

indicators.note: without in its old sense of outside, so the word for married goes round

parts.note: wed means married

indicators.note: twice means the letter for love appears two times

parts.note: love is zero in tennis, which looks like the letter O

explanation.surface: Courted a lover and wed in a loveless marriage two times over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without' is used in its old sense of outside, not lacking; tennis scores love as zero, which looks like O.
explanation.definitionFit: To press one's suit is to court someone in hope of marriage.

definitions.meaning: a duty or charge imposed
to ... troops is to enlist them compulsorily

explanation.definitionFit: A charge imposed by authority, and to raise soldiers compulsorily.

indicators.note: one slips inside the church body, as an infiltrator gets in

parts.note: the nave is the main body of a church
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A trusting congregation into which a spy creeps.
explanation.walkthrough: 'church body' is not a congregation but the nave, the main part of the building.
explanation.definitionFit: Innocent and trusting, lacking guile or worldly wariness.

clue.text: Volume of Aristotle — I can't understand any of it

definitions.meaning: a book by a Greek philosopher

definitions.text: I can't understand any of it
definitions.meaning: the idiom for something incomprehensible

explanation.definitionFit: The idiom for total incomprehension, also read as a philosophical book from ancient Athens.

clue.text: Learned to be devious about reported capture

indicators.note: about means the word for devious goes around the rest

parts.note: sly means devious

indicators.note: reported signals that the word for capture is heard rather than spelt

parts.note: to collar someone is to capture them

explanation.surface: Learning to be sneaky around a reported arrest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'reported' signals the sound-alike: the capture word is heard, then 'about' wraps the devious word around it.
explanation.definitionFit: Erudite, having much academic knowledge.

clue.text: Oldest man was quizzed about role in Great War

definitions.text: Oldest man was quizzed about role in Great War

parts.words: Oldest man was quizzed about role in Great War
parts.note: a famous First World War recruiting poster shows a child asking a father what he did in the Great War

explanation.surface: A very old veteran interviewed about his part in the First World War.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Oldest man' suggests a centenarian; it is the 'old man' (father) of the poster 'What did you do in the Great War?'
explanation.definitionFit: Childish word for father, the parent questioned on the famous recruiting poster.
